subject: Critical Thinking
title: Confirmation Bias: Seeing What You Already Believe
description: A short lesson to help you apply Confirmation Bias: Seeing What You Already Believe.

hook.text: You search Google for 'coffee is healthy.' You find 50 studies confirming it. Search over. Bias complete.

buildup.text: Confirmation bias: we seek, notice, and remember evidence that supports what we already believe.

discovery.text: Peter Wason proved it in 1960. People tested rules by looking for confirming cases — almost never disconfirming ones.

twist.text: Social media amplifies it exponentially. Algorithms feed you content you agree with — a bias machine.

climax.text: The antidote: actively seek evidence against your belief. If it survives, your belief is stronger.

punchline.text: The strongest beliefs are the ones that survived attack.

quiz.question: What is confirmation bias?
options: Seeking and favoring evidence that supports existing beliefs

details.summary: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret, and remember information that supports your existing beliefs while ignoring contradictory evidence. It is arguably the most pervasive cognitive bias.
details.whyItMatters: Confirmation bias distorts research, politics, relationships, and personal decisions. It turns your brain into a filter that reinforces whatever you already think.
takeaways: We actively seek evidence that confirms our beliefs
Contradictory evidence is dismissed or reinterpreted
Confirmation bias operates in selection, interpretation, and memory

faq.question: How does confirmation bias affect how we search for information?
faq.answer: You are more likely to click on articles that agree with you, follow accounts that share your views, and phrase search queries in ways that confirm your hypothesis. The bias shapes what information you encounter.

faq.question: What is the most effective technique for fighting confirmation bias?
faq.answer: Actively seek out the strongest arguments against your position. Ask yourself what evidence would change your mind, and genuinely look for it. This forced perspective-taking counteracts the bias.
